title: The Book of the Tales — Akwụkwọ Ifo
description: The stories the people tell: the tortoise and the feast above, the mosquito and the ear, the sun and the moon, the drum and the fire, the two brothers and the land, the child who asked why. The teaching is inside the story, not beside it.
html:
BOOK OF THE TALES (Akwụkwọ Ifo)

A book of the stories the people tell. They are not history and they are not law. They are the way a thing is remembered when it is remembered by a grandmother, and the teaching is inside the story and not beside it.

Chapter 1 — Mbà, the Tortoise, and the Feast Above

1 Mbà the tortoise was a man of appetite and a man of a small shell, and this is the story of how the shell came to be cracked.

2 There was a feast in the sky, and the birds were invited. Mbà was not invited, for the sky-dwellers did not count a tortoise among the flying things. And Mbà went to the birds and said: "Lend me a feather each, and let me come with you, and I will be your spokesman, and I will speak well of you at the feast."

3 And the birds, who are vain, lent him a feather each, and he was covered in feathers, and he looked like a bird, and he flew with them. And the birds said: "When we arrive, what shall we be called?" And Mbà said: "You shall be called All of you." And they agreed.

4 And when they came to the sky, the host asked: "Who are these?" And Mbà stepped forward and said: "I am All of you." And the host said: "Then All of you shall eat first."

5 And Mbà ate the food of all of them, and the birds were left with the scraps, and each bird took back its feather, and they flew home and left him there.

6 And Mbà looked down at the ground and did not know how to reach it. And he called to the birds to carry a message to his wife: "Bring out the soft things, and spread them under the compound, that I may fall on them." And the birds carried the message, and the parrot — who had not forgotten the feast — carried it crooked, and said to Mbà's wife: "Bring out the hard things, and spread them under the compound."

7 And she brought out the mortar and the pestle and the hoes and the knives, and she spread them under the compound. And Mbà fell, and fell a long time, and came down upon the hard things, and his shell was cracked in pieces.

8 And his wife took the pieces and put them together, and they held, and the seams are there yet. And this is why the tortoise's shell is a map of a broken thing that was mended.

9 The teaching: he who eats alone eats a broken shell. The one who takes the portion of all of them will find no one to carry his message truly.

Chapter 2 — The Mosquito and the Ear

1 The mosquito has no house and no farm, and this is why he lives in the ear of man.

2 In the beginning the mosquito was a woman, and she was married, and she was a wife of a certain man, and she had one complaint: the husband would not speak to her. He came in and he sat and he ate and he slept, and he spoke to no one, and least of all to her.

3 And the mosquito-woman said to the ear of the husband: "You hear everything and you say nothing. I will come and live in you, and I will be the one who speaks." And she asked the ear for a place, and the ear agreed, for the ear is generous and keeps no gate.

4 And ever since, the mosquito goes into the ear of man and speaks, and it is the one sound that never asks leave, because it was given leave once, and the leave was never taken back.

5 The teaching: a word kept too long will find a tongue that was never meant for it. The husband who said nothing did not keep peace; he lost the inside of his own head to a small noise.

Chapter 3 — The Sun and the Moon

1 The sun and the moon were once one house, and they were not easy with each other.

2 And the moon said: "You burn, and you go out and everything looks, and I am left with the night." And the sun said: "Then take the night, and I will keep the day, and let us not meet, for there is no hour in which we agree."

3 And the moon said one thing before she went: "When I am thin, know that I am turning away; and when I am full, know that I have come back whole." And she showed him her seasons: the new moon, the first quarter, the full, and the old.

4 And the people saw it, and learned to count the moon, and learned that a going-away is not the same thing as an end. And this is why a household counts a month by the moon and not by the sun.

5 The teaching: a parting that keeps its word is a coming-back. The moon never promised to stay. She promised to return, and she has kept it every month since.

Chapter 4 — The Drum, the Fire and the Word

1 In the beginning the people had no drum, and they called to one another from hill to hill, and the calling was slow.

2 And a woman found that the skin of a goat stretched over the mouth of a clay pot made a sound that carried further than the voice, and she showed it to her husband, and the husband showed it to the town, and the town said: this is a new mouth and it must be taught to speak.

3 And they named the kinds of speech the drum would have: the call from one compound to the next; the cry that a death has happened; the call to market; the call to the shrine; and the call to war, which is the one that is most careful. For the drum can begin a thing that no one can stop, and so the man who holds the drum is chosen for his restraint and not for his strength.

4 And the fire was already there, and the fire was older than the drum. And the people said: the fire is the first word and the drum is the second, for the fire can be seen from far and the drum can be heard from far, and the two together mean the town is awake and no one is alone.

5 The teaching: a mouth that can be heard everywhere must be a mouth under law. The drum is not the loudest thing in the town. It is the most careful.

Chapter 5 — The Two Brothers and the Land

1 Two brothers were given one field by their father, and the father said: "Divide it and be neighbours."

2 And the elder brother took the side with the stream, and the younger took the side with the slope, and both said the other had done better.

3 And they took it to the elders, and the elders went to look, and saw that the stream would dry in the harmattan and the slope would wash in the first rain, and that neither part was whole, and that the field had been one field and had been cut in two, and that the cutting was the whole of the trouble.

4 And the elders said: "Put the fence back where your father had it, and work the field together, and take the harvest by turns: this year the stream side eats first, next year the slope side." And it was done, and the field was whole again, and the brothers remained brothers.

5 The teaching: a field divided is two fields and neither is enough. The fathers of the town did not ask who was right. They asked what the land could carry.

Chapter 6 — The Child Who Asked Why

1 A child asked his grandmother why the people greet the morning, and the grandmother did not answer, and the child asked again.

2 And the grandmother said: "Go out and stand at the door when the sky is turning, and tell me what you see." And the child went, and came back, and said: "I saw nothing. It was dark and then it was not dark."

3 And the grandmother said: "That is the whole of it." And she said: "There is no hour when the dark learns it has lost. It is dark, and then it is not. And a man is the same: he does not feel himself turning. So we greet the morning aloud, so that the turning is marked, and so that a person who has lived through a dark night hears that the night has ended and is told it aloud."

4 And from that day the child greeted the morning. And this is why the greeting is not for the sky. It is for the person who is standing in the doorway beside you.

5 The teaching: a day is not new until it is said to be new. The greeting is the way a man is told, out loud, that he has come through.

Here ends the Book of the Tales. The stories are the people's own, told at evening in the compound, and the book keeps them because a people is its stories as much as its law.
